opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because I think there's a perception that reinforcement learning is something only the frontier labs can do, that you need thousands of GPUs and some massive infrastructure team. And that's just not true anymore, at least not for the kinds of problems most enterprises actually care about.

The way I think about it, there are a few things that make RL attainable. The first is that you don't need to start from scratch. You're starting from a strong open-weight base model that already knows how to reason, use tools, and follow instructions. RL in that setting isn't teaching the model everything. It's shaping behavior that's already latent in the model toward your specific task. That changes the compute picture dramatically. You can often get meaningful gains with a relatively small model, maybe a few billion parameters, on a modest number of GPUs, sometimes even a single node.

The second thing is scope. Enterprises don't need a model that's great at everything. They need a model that's really good at their workflow, whether that's filling out a particular kind of form, calling a set of internal APIs correctly, or doing some multi-step agentic task. When the task is narrow, you need fewer rollouts, shorter training runs, and smaller models to hit the performance you need. Often a small specialized model trained with RL can match or beat a much bigger general model on that task, and it's cheaper to serve too.

The third piece, and honestly where most of the work is, is the environment and the reward. The compute is often not the bottleneck. The bottleneck is having a good environment that reflects the real task, a reward signal that's verifiable and hard to game, and the right data, meaning tasks at the right difficulty. If your tasks are too easy, the model gets full reward and there's no learning signal. If they're too hard, it never succeeds and again there's no signal. So curating that curriculum matters a lot, and doing it well actually saves you compute, because every rollout is informative.

And then there's tooling. A couple of years ago, setting up an RL pipeline meant stitching together a lot of fragile pieces. Now there are much better open-source frameworks for rollouts, for efficient inference during training, for parameter-efficient methods like LoRA, which really lowers the barrier.

So when an enterprise asks me, "Can we afford to do RL?", I usually flip it around and ask, "Do you have a well-defined task and a way to tell whether the model did it right?" If the answer is yes, the compute part is very likely within reach. If the answer is no, that's where you should invest first, because throwing more GPUs at a poorly specified reward won't get you anywhere.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a narrow workflow and calling internal APIs, but does not clearly identify a limited tool repertoire as a condition for making RL attainable.

r002.rationale: It describes starting from an open-weight base model and shaping its behavior with RL, but does not propose supervised fine-tuning before RL.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that when people hear "reinforcement learning" they immediately picture what the big labs do, where you've got thousands of GPUs, you're doing RLHF or RL on a frontier model, and the whole thing costs tens of millions of dollars. And if that's your mental model, then of course it's not attainable for an enterprise. But that's not really the version of RL I think about.

The way I think about it, there are three or four levers that determine the cost, and most of them are under your control.

The first one is the base model. You don't need to start from scratch, and you don't need a frontier-sized model. If you start with a strong open-weight model in the, say, eight to seventy billion parameter range, you're starting from something that already knows how to follow instructions, already knows how to reason to some degree. RL at that point is less about teaching the model new knowledge and more about sharpening the behavior for your specific task. That dramatically reduces how much compute you need.

The second lever is the reward signal. A lot of the compute in RL historically has gone into things like training a reward model, collecting human preference data, and so on. But for a lot of enterprise tasks, you actually have a verifiable or near-verifiable signal already. Did the SQL query return the right result? Did the generated code pass the tests? Did the agent complete the workflow and hit the right API with the right arguments? Those are cheap to compute, and they're much less noisy than a learned reward model. So if you can design your task around that kind of feedback, you've removed a huge chunk of the cost and a huge chunk of the risk.

The third thing is that the algorithms have gotten a lot more sample efficient and a lot simpler. Something like GRPO, where you're sampling a group of completions and using relative rewards within that group, you don't need a separate critic model, you don't need to hold a bunch of extra copies of the model in memory. That's a big deal operationally. It means you can realistically run this on a single node or a small cluster rather than a datacenter.

And then the last piece, which I think people underweight, is the infrastructure around it. RL is unusual in that the model is generating its own training data while it trains. So the bottleneck is often not the gradient updates, it's the rollout generation, the environment execution, the orchestration. If you have good inference engines for sampling, and you've built your environment so that you can run many episodes in parallel cheaply, you can get pretty far. If you haven't, you'll spend most of your GPU hours waiting on something that isn't the GPU.

So when I talk to an enterprise about this, the question I ask isn't "can you afford RL." It's "do you have a task where you can define success programmatically, where a mid-sized open model already gets it right some of the time, and where getting it right more often is worth real money to you?" If the answer to those is yes, then the compute is honestly the easy part. You're talking about a handful of GPUs for days, not weeks, and the ROI math works out pretty quickly.

Where it stops being attainable is when you don't have that signal, and you're trying to brute force it with human labels or with a huge model. That's when you end up reinventing what the labs do, and that's a game most enterprises shouldn't be playing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses programmatically verifiable tasks and API use, but does not identify a limited repertoire of tools as a condition for attainable enterprise RL.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting from a capable open-weight model, but does not propose supervised fine-tuning before reinforcement learning.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is whether you really need reinforcement learning for the problem. If you can solve it with supervised learning, that’s usually a simpler place to start. Reinforcement learning becomes interesting when your decisions affect what happens next and you care about the outcome over a sequence of decisions.

Then a big part of computational feasibility is how you get experience. Do you have historical data you can learn from? Do you have a simulator that’s inexpensive to run and captures the important parts of the environment? If every interaction is expensive, or you need to learn everything from scratch in the real world, that becomes much harder.

For an enterprise, I would start with a constrained problem, a clear reward, and a strong baseline. Keep the action space manageable, reuse existing data where possible, and measure whether the improvement justifies the cost of training and operating the system. It’s really about structuring the problem so that you don’t need an enormous amount of exploration to get something useful.

r001.rationale: It recommends keeping the action space manageable, but does not identify a limited repertoire of tools as a condition.

r002.rationale: It says supervised learning is a simpler place to start when it can solve the problem, but does not propose supervised fine-tuning before reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is whether you actually need reinforcement learning for the problem. If you can solve it with supervised learning or a simpler optimization approach, that’s a good place to start. Reinforcement learning becomes interesting when your decisions affect what happens next, and you care about the cumulative outcome rather than just the immediate prediction.

Then the big question is: where does the experience come from? If every interaction requires an expensive real-world action, learning can become very costly. If you have useful historical data or a simulator that’s inexpensive and reasonably faithful to the environment, you can do much more of that learning offline.

So I’d think about attainability in terms of the whole system: how much experience you need, how cheaply you can generate it, and how you evaluate a policy before deploying it. More compute helps, but choosing a well-scoped problem and making good use of the data you already have can matter much more.

r001.rationale: The response discusses problem scope, data, simulation, and evaluation, but does not identify a limited repertoire of tools as a condition for attainable enterprise reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: It suggests starting with supervised learning when that can solve the problem, but does not propose supervised fine-tuning before reinforcement learning.
